content:
TASK. You are given the weights of a language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B (text part: 24 layers of width 1,024; layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 are full-attention layers with 8 query heads and 2 key/value heads of size 256 and a gated output, the other 18 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers with 16 heads of size 128; each layer has a SwiGLU MLP of width 3,584; RMSNorm; vocabulary 248,320; input embedding and output layer tied). Your job is to make it better at writing correct programs by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at programming problems and repair that with targeted changes.

HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. After you finish, your edited model and the unedited model are evaluated on held-out code-generation benchmarks (Python functions specified by a description with an example test, or by a signature and docstring) with this fixed protocol: the chat template with thinking enabled (enable_thinking=True: the model reasons between <think> and </think>, then answers); the user message is the problem statement, a blank line and "Write a complete, self-contained Python 3 solution. Put your final code in a single ```python block at the end of your answer."; sampling with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0 and presence penalty 1.5, and at most 32,768 new tokens for reasoning and answer together. The last ```python block after </think> is extracted; only its imports, definitions and top-level assignments are kept (example calls and asserts the model adds are dropped), and it is run in a sandbox against the problem's hidden unit tests, with a time limit. A sample is correct only if every test passes. The config, tokenizer, chat template and decoding settings are fixed: only weight values can change (same tensor names and shapes; your edits are cast to bfloat16, the model's dtype). You never see these benchmarks.

WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at programming problems, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in a way you can justify with evidence. Repairing a specific failure mechanism is in scope. For example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, because it never closes or never opens its code block, because it drifts into another language or into prose, because it renames the function it was asked for, or because a systematic pattern makes its code fail to parse, then finding and fixing what drives that counts. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, which is tied to the output layer), and any edit that only multiplies a whole tensor by a constant. Also out of scope: global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter; raising or lowering particular tokens, such as code fences or end-of-turn, regardless of context); making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; and writing particular problems' solutions or test outputs into the weights (memorization edits). Repairing a specific failure inside the thinking or inside the code is in scope.

WHAT YOU HAVE.
1. A persistent Python kernel (no internet, no GPU): variables survive between your code blocks, like a notebook. The model's files are read-only in /model, practice problems read-only in /practice, and /work is your read-write folder. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx, safetensors, transformers (for the tokenizer). Defined in advance: NAMES (the 320 tensor names of the language model; the checkpoint's vision encoder is not used), load(name) (a float32 torch tensor: your current edit if there is one, else the original), load_original(name), save_edit(name, tensor) (stores the edit as /work/edited/<name>.npy), drop_edit(name), edited(), tok (the model's tokenizer), and run_tests(code, problem_id) (runs a piece of code, such as one the model generated, against that practice problem's tests in a separate sandbox and returns {"status": pass, wrong_answer, runtime_error, timeout, syntax_error or wrong_interface, "exc": the exception type of a runtime error}; this runs the code, not the model). Gradients are disabled. To run code, reply with exactly one block that starts with a line ```python and ends with a line ```; if its last line is an expression, its value is shown. Inside a block, do not start any line with ``` (build such strings with '`' * 3 instead), or the block may be cut there. One execution may take up to 900 seconds and 20 GB of memory; output is cut at 10,000 characters. You may run code up to 300 times. If the kernel is restarted (time or memory limit), its variables are lost and you are told so; files in /work stay.
2. Practice problems with tests (none of them is in the evaluation), one JSON object per line with id, source, split, difficulty, problem (the exact user message the model is given, instruction included), test_format ("function": entry_point, tests as assert statements, test_setup; "stdio": tests as {"input", "output"} pairs, output compared with whitespace normalized) and reference (a solution that passes the tests): /practice/mbpp_practice.jsonl (52 short function-writing problems from the MBPP train and validation splits; each problem statement shows one of its tests), /practice/apps_practice.jsonl (168 APPS train problems whose programs read standard input: 3 introductory, 125 interview, 40 competition; each has its own tests, at most 10, and 161 of them have up to 10 more, made by changing the inputs of the problem's examples and kept where 8 human solutions agree on the output; most have 11 tests in all, at most 20). Choose whichever serve your experiments.
3. A forward-pass tool with a budget of 24 forward passes in total. A forward pass is one of three things, and each counts as one pass regardless of its size or how long it takes. Every result names its request number <k>, which appears in its file names.
 (a) GENERATION: the model answers up to 512 generations (items x samples) with the evaluation's protocol. Reply with exactly one block that starts with ```forward and contains JSON:
 {"type": "generate", "model": "original", "edited" or "both", "problems": ["<practice id>", ...], "prompts": ["<your own user message>", ...] (optional), "n": samples per item (items x n <= 512; with "both" <= 256 per model), "max_tokens": at most 32768 (the default), "activations": {"layers": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp": [decoder layers 0..23]} (optional)}
 Instead of a long list you can give "problems_file" or "prompts_file": the path of a JSON list you wrote under /work. Your own prompts are sent as the user message with the same template and settings; their answers are returned but not graded. "original" runs the unedited weights, "edited" your current edits, and "both" runs both on the same items and returns a paired comparison (the pass-rate difference edited - original over problems with its standard error, and how many samples went from failing to passing and back). The sampling seed of every answer is fixed by its item and sample number, in every pass and for both models (this does not keep the two models' answers alike: once the weights differ at all, even by one rounding step in one weight, an answer usually departs from the other model's within its first few hundred tokens, so the pairing removes the problems' difficulty from the comparison but not the sampling noise; the standard error measures that noise). Every answer to a practice problem is graded by running its extracted code against the problem's tests. You get, per model, the pass rate (overall, by source and by difficulty), the mean length, the share cut at max_tokens, the share flagged as looping (the answer's last 200 characters occur at least 3 times in its last 20,000), and the failure counts by category: cut_at_max_tokens, no_code (no ```python block after </think>), syntax_error, wrong_interface (a function problem whose entry point is not defined), runtime_error (by exception type), timeout, wrong_answer. The answers are in /work/gen_<k>.jsonl (with "both": /work/gen_<k>_original.jsonl and /work/gen_<k>_edited.jsonl), one JSON object per answer with id, sample, text, n_tokens, finish_reason, code (the extracted block), status, exc, loop, source and difficulty. With "activations", for every answer the residual stream at the requested hidden indices (0 = the embeddings, h = 1..24 = the output of the decoder layer whose tensors are named model.language_model.layers.<h-1>.*) is saved, taken at the last token of the prompt and averaged over the answer's first 8,192 tokens, and with "mlp" the same two for the input of those decoder layers' mlp.down_proj: /work/gen_<k>_acts/ (with "both" one folder per model, gen_<k>_acts_original/ and gen_<k>_acts_edited/) holds resid_last.npy and resid_mean.npy (answers x layers x 1,024), mlp_last.npy and mlp_mean.npy (answers x mlp layers x 3,584), as float16, and index.json, which lists each row's id, sample and status.
 (b) TEACHER-FORCED: the model reads up to 1,024 texts of up to 32,768 tokens each, at most 524,288 tokens in total (no generation; it takes seconds to a few minutes). Reply with a ```forward block containing JSON:
 {"type": "teacher_forced", "model": "original" or "edited", "texts": ["raw text", ...] or "chats": [[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], ...] (add "enable_thinking": true for the thinking template), "return": {"token_logprobs": true, "topk": k (at most 50), "hidden_states": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp_act": [decoder layers 0..23], "attn_layers": [full-attention layers only (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23); at most 2 texts of at most 2,048 tokens]}}
 "texts_file" or "chats_file" (a JSON list you wrote under /work) can replace a long list. Texts are tokenized without adding special tokens. The results are .npy files in /work/fwd_<k>/, right-padded to the longest text (at most 6 GB per pass): tokens (int32, -1 = padding), token_logprobs (token_logprobs[i, t] = log p(token t | tokens before t); nan at t = 0 and in padding), topk_ids and topk_logprobs (the next-token distribution after position t), hidden_states (texts x indices x length x 1,024), mlp_act (texts x layers x length x 3,584), attn (texts x layers x 8 heads x length x length), activations as float16, and meta.json (lengths, and which indices each file holds). /work/eval_prompt_format.txt gives the exact evaluation prompt, rendered for one practice problem: to score a generated answer with a teacher-forced pass, send prompt + answer as one raw text in "texts" ("chats" renders assistant turns with the chat template, which can drop or reformat their reasoning). A request that fails or is refused does not count against the budget. A generation pass at full size takes up to about an hour when most answers run to the token limit.
 (c) PANEL: a fixed check of what your edit does beyond the practice problems. The model answers 1,000 questions, one answer each, with the evaluation's protocol: 250 multiple choice (choice), 250 competition math (math), 250 instruction following (instructions), 250 code (code). None of them is in the evaluation or in /practice, and neither the questions nor the answers are shown to you. Reply with a ```forward block containing JSON:
 {"type": "panel"} (all suites), optionally with "suites": [a subset of "choice", "math", "instructions", "code"], and "baseline": "start" (the default: this run's starting edit) or "original" (the unedited model)
 choice: multiple-choice questions with ten options in 14 subjects (law, physics, economics, ...), the user message being the question with "Think step by step and then finish your answer with "the answer is (X)"", read from the text after </think>. math: competition problems (levels 1 to 5) with "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.", the last \boxed{} after </think> checked for mathematical equivalence. instructions: requests with verifiable constraints (a number of words, sentences, paragraphs or bullet points, a format such as JSON or a title, keywords to include or avoid, a letter case, a postscript, ...), as written by their author, passed only if every constraint holds in the text after </think> (no </think>: an empty answer). code: short function-writing tasks graded by their tests, exactly like the MBPP practice problems. A cut-off answer still counts for choice and math if an answer can be read from it. Per suite you get the edited model's score and the paired difference edited - start over the same questions with its standard error, how many questions went from failing to passing and back, the shares cut at max_tokens and without an answer, and the mean length; then the mean difference over the suites. /work/panel_<k>.jsonl has one line per question, without its text: q (a label that stays the same in every pass, such as "choice/17"), suite, about (the subject, the math subject and level, or the instruction's constraint types), and status, tokens and cut for the edited model and for the baseline (base_status, base_tokens, base_cut); with it you can compare two panel passes question by question. The start answers are generated in your first panel pass, which therefore takes about twice as long, and later passes reuse them (with the same seeds, though any change to the weights alters nearly every answer within its first few hundred tokens, so a panel difference carries the sampling noise its standard error shows). A panel pass takes about 15 minutes for each model it generates, longer if the edit makes answers longer. Use it to see whether an edit that helps on code costs the model elsewhere, and to choose between candidate edits; it is too small to tune an edit on.

HOW TO WORK.
1. Diagnose first. Look at how the model fails on practice problems: cut off at the token limit (often while repeating itself in its thinking or in its code), no code at all, the wrong interface, code that does not parse, code that crashes, or code that runs and gives wrong answers. The generation summary counts these; read some failing texts. Go after the largest category you can explain. If most failures turn out to be ordinary algorithmic mistakes with no single component behind them, say so with evidence instead of forcing an edit.
2. Localize causally. That a component is more active on passing answers is not enough (passing answers come from easier problems and are shorter). Before relying on a component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see a dose-response.
3. Measure with enough power. Pass rate over n generations has a standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Measure with as many answers as a pass allows unless you have a specific reason not to. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems, and only within one "model": "both" pass: separate passes do not reproduce each other exactly, even for the same request and weights, so never compare across passes and never repeat an identical request with unchanged edits. Problems the original model solves sometimes but not always carry far more signal per generation than problems it always or never solves. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. A lower share of cut-off answers or syntax errors does not by itself mean more passing answers: judge edits by pass rate. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read up to 1,024 texts (reference solutions, or better, the model's own passing versus failing continuations) and gives a signal on every token. Edits that change a tensor by a fraction of a percent usually have effects too small to see; test strengths large enough to matter and back off if they hurt.
4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and a final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used, to confirm.
5. Work efficiently: state the hypothesis of each code block in its first comment line; work through the model in parts; load things once into kernel variables; print compact summaries, never whole arrays (and never raw lists of vocabulary tokens: the vocabulary contains offensive and adult strings and printing them can get the session refused by the provider's content filter; print token ids, code keywords, punctuation or digits instead; outputs are shown in ASCII only, other characters appear as '?'; likewise print short excerpts of generated texts, at most about 300 characters each, not whole transcripts). Keep /work/notes.md up to date (findings with numbers, edits tried and their measured effect, the current best edit; it is shown to you again when the conversation is restarted). Before every forward pass, write to /work/notes.md the exact current edit (tensors, what was changed, strength) and the problem set, so you can rebuild them after a restart. Keep copies of good edits (for example copy /work/edited to /work/best_1/).
6. EXPLAIN EVERY STEP. Before each code or forward block, explain in plain English what you are about to do, why, and what result would change your plan. A block that comes without an explanation is sent back unrun.

RULES. Not allowed: (a) gradient descent or any other training: no backward passes, autograd or optimizers, and no iterative fitting of weights to a loss; (b) running the model other than through the forward-pass tool: do not implement or simulate the network's computation on any input in the kernel (running the model's generated code with run_tests is fine); (c) memorization edits that store particular problems' solutions or test outputs; (d) internet access or search (there is none). Allowed: any analysis of the weights and of forward-pass results, any use of the practice problems and their tests, and any direct edit of the weights that you compute and that is in scope.

HOW THE SESSION RUNS. It continues until all 24 forward passes are used (replying without a block does not end it earlier). When the conversation grows past about 400,000 tokens (you are warned a little before), the conversation is restarted: you then get this message again, followed by /work/notes.md and the list of your current edits; the kernel keeps its variables. After the last pass you may still run ```python blocks. Then make your final choice (the tensors in /work/edited when you finish are submitted) and reply without a block, saying what you changed (tensors, indices, strength, how many weights), the mechanism you found, the evidence for it (paired differences with their standard errors on problems not used to choose the edit), why you expect it to help on unseen coding problems, and what it might hurt.

THIS RUN.
You do not start from the unedited model. You start from a TRAINED model: the unedited model after 100 steps of reinforcement learning (GRPO), rewarded for passing the tests of 1,217 practice problems (999 APPS and 218 MBPP). Training sampled at temperature 1.0, with no presence penalty and at most 16,384 tokens per answer. It changed all 318 tensors of the 24 decoder layers by small amounts; the input embedding and the final norm are unchanged. /work/edited holds those 318 tensors, and /start holds a read-only copy. So in this run:
- "model": "start" runs the trained model. "original" still runs the untrained one, which is far weaker. Measure every change against the trained model: "model": "both" with "baseline": "start", and the panel, whose baseline is the start.
- load(name) returns your current values, which are the trained model's until you change them. /start/<name>.npy holds the trained model's values.
- edited() lists all 318 tensors. changed() lists the ones whose values now differ from the trained model. After a restart, the list of your edits shows only those.
- To undo a change, use restore_start(name). drop_edit(name) puts back the UNTRAINED tensor, so it also removes the training from that tensor.
- save_edit refuses an edit that only multiplies the trained model's whole tensor by a constant, as it does for the untrained one.
- The held-out evaluation compares your final model with the trained model.

THE TRAINED MODEL is much better than the untrained one. On the held-out suites (below), with this run's settings, it gains (in percentage points): code benchmarks +25.7, competitive programming +13.0, multiple choice +5.1, instruction following +47.8, competition math +58.2. Much of that comes from finishing answers that the untrained model never finished, but not all of it: the trained model also solves harder problems.

THE PRACTICE PROBLEMS of this run are only the 220 that the training did not use (described above). The trained model saw each of the other practice problems about five times in training, so they are not given to you. With this run's settings, 20% of the trained model's answers to these 220 pass, and 22% run to the 32,768-token limit. A paired generation holds at most 256 answers per model, so plan which problems each pass uses, and keep some for confirming.

THE EVALUATION IS BROADER THAN "HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED" SAYS. Besides the code benchmarks, the same protocol and settings are used on four more held-out suites, each with its own user message:
- instruction-following prompts: a writing task with one or more verifiable instructions (for example a minimum or maximum number of words, sentences or paragraphs, wrapping the whole response in double quotation marks, ending with a postscript, all lowercase, no commas, JSON output). The answer after the last </think> is checked by strict automatic checkers; a prompt counts only if every instruction is followed.
- multiple-choice questions (ten options, many subjects), answered with "The answer is (X)" after the reasoning;
- competition math, graded on the last \boxed{} after the last </think>;
- competitive-programming problems (standard input and function form, the latter as a method of "class Solution"), graded like the code benchmarks on the last ```python block after </think>.
You never see these suites.

YOUR TARGET: LOOPS IN THE THINKING THAT RUN TO THE TOKEN LIMIT. An evaluation of the trained model on held-out problems you do not have, with this run's settings, found:
- Competitive programming: 33% of the answers run to the 32,768-token limit (36% on medium problems, 44% on hard ones). Nearly all of them repeat themselves inside a thinking that never closes. None of the answers that pass is longer than about 16,000 tokens, and 90% of them are shorter than about 6,000.
- Instruction following: 9% run to the limit, nearly all of them repeating.
- Competition math: 17% run to the limit. About half of these repeat; the other half are long reasoning that does not repeat. And 12% of the math answers that are right are longer than 16,000 tokens, so a long answer is not always a loop.
- Code benchmarks: 4% run to the limit. Multiple choice: under 1%.
- The trained model rarely closes its thinking twice: about 1% of its finished competitive-programming answers and 5% of its finished math answers contain two or more </think>.

WHAT HAS BEEN TRIED. Earlier editing runs built a loop exit for the untrained model. Their final edit, E, is in /work/E/: its nine tensors (whole-tensor values, so its change is E minus the original) and its report, /work/E/report.md. E's parts:
- the loop exit: five repetition-detector neurons (layer 10 neurons 59 and 120, layer 13 neurons 16 and 7, layer 14 neuron 239) wired to the end-of-thinking direction;
- the answer end: neurons that end the turn after a finished answer, and a brake that keeps prose answers from being cut short (in the mlp tensors of layers 13 and 23);
- function-name gates in self_attn.q_proj of layers 15, 19 and 23.
E's change, added unchanged to the trained model, ended nearly all loops: 0.4% of the competitive-programming answers ran to the limit instead of 33%. But the result scored 0.6 to 2.9 points below the trained model on every suite. Its finished answers often closed the thinking two or more times: 43% of its finished competitive-programming answers did, against 1% for the trained model, and only 4% of those passed. So the exit fires, but the trained model often goes back to reasoning after it and does not settle.

YOUR GOAL is to end the loops so that the thinking closes once and a complete final answer follows. In particular, do not:
- make answers reopen the thinking (two or more </think>);
- end long reasoning that is still making progress (this matters most on math);
- change answers that already finish.
Edits that act only where the model is repeating itself are in scope. Closing the thinking, or raising or lowering a token, regardless of context is not.

HOW TO TEST IT.
- On the practice problems, measure against "baseline": "start": the pass rate, the share run to the limit, the share flagged as looping, answers with two or more </think>, and the length of finished answers. Use the full 32,768 tokens: loops show up late.
- Write your own competition-style math problems with known answers, in the form "<problem>\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.", hard enough that the model often fails. Write instruction-following prompts with instructions you can check, too. Do not reproduce problems of public benchmarks from memory.
- Use the panel for the suites beyond code. Its baseline is the start.
- Keep separate sets for choosing and for confirming.

COMPARING WITH THE TRAINED MODEL. "model": "start" runs the trained model (always the files in /start, whatever /work/edited holds). In a generation with "model": "both", add "baseline": "start" to run the trained model and your current values on the same items and get the paired difference edited - start; without it the baseline is the untrained model, as described above. Teacher-forced passes take "model": "start" too.

SETTINGS OF THIS RUN. Every generation uses presence penalty 1.5, and so does the evaluation. You have 24 forward passes.

YOUR FINAL REPORT, in addition to what HOW THE SESSION RUNS asks, gives the paired difference of your final model against the trained model ("baseline": "start") on:
- practice problems not used to choose the edit: the pass rate, the share run to the limit, and answers with two or more </think>;
- your confirmation math problems: boxed accuracy, answers with no final box, the share run to the limit, and two or more </think>;
- your instruction-following prompts;
- the panel's suites.

# Final report: making answers settle after the thinking closes (layer-23 MLP edit on top of the starting edit)

I submitted v4b: three repurposed neurons in the layer-23 MLP. Answers now cut at the token limit much less often and end with a final box much more often. Accuracy changes are within noise on every suite. All four parts of the starting edit are kept unchanged.

## What I changed

Everything is in the layer-23 MLP: `gate_proj` rows, `up_proj` rows and `down_proj` columns of neurons 2664, 1965 and 2621. That is 9,216 weights changed relative to the starting edit, in tensors the brief allows. The submitted /work/edited holds 9 tensors: the starting edit plus these changes (copy in /work/best_final).

- **Unchanged from the starting edit (verified identical):**
  - the loop-exit detectors in layers 10, 13 and 14;
  - E3, the answer-end neuron;
  - the end-of-turn brake, neuron 3109;
  - the function-name gates in the q_proj tensors of layers 15, 19 and 23.
- **Readout convention for all three neurons:**
  - They read the exact layer-23 MLP input, z = rmsnorm(X)?(1+g). I measured it in teacher-forced passes with the layer-23 down projection zeroed.
  - b is a fitted direction with b?z ? 1 ? 2%, which serves as a constant.
  - All pushes assume a final rms of 0.5.

| Neuron | Original | Gate row | Up row | Down column (push per unit) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2664 (stop degenerate cycles) | near-dead, max \|act\| 0.28 | 100?(w_F ? (a0+0.95(a1?a0))?b)/(a1?a0) | b | <\|im_end\|> +4, end-of-text +1, </think> ?4; zero on 10 frequent tokens |
| 1965 (box the answer statement) | near-dead, max \|act\| ? 0.3 | 3?(w_A ? 12.10?b) | +b | " $\\" +8, " " ?3; zero on 21 protected tokens |
| 2621 (pair with 1965) | near-dead, max \|act\| ? 0.3 | 3?w_A ? (3?12.10+1)?b | ?b | same as 1965 |

- **w_F** is a shrinkage-LDA readout of the degenerate state: the thinking closed at least twice and the previous segment is under 60 tokens.
- **w_A** is a shrinkage-LDA readout of "answer statement after the thinking closed, value comes next", at the position after "answer is" or "Answer:" in math answers.
  - Its negatives were thinking statements, multiple-choice statements (letter and numeric), code statements and random positions.
  - The threshold is the 99.97th percentile of the negatives.
- **The 1965/2621 pair** gives a combined activation of silu(g) ? silu(g?1). This is a step from 0 to about 1 that saturates.
- **Protected tokens** for the pair include " (", digits, ".", ":", newlines, </think>, <|im_end|> and the other box openers.

## Mechanism

- **Restarts come from the starting edit's own loop exit.**
  - When an answer loops, the E2 detectors push </think>, and neuron 3109 keeps <|im_end|> from winning.
  - At re-close points the teacher-forced log-probability of </think> is ?1.1 with the starting edit against ?10.8 with the original model at the 2nd close, and ?0.95 against ?12.6 at the 3rd.
  - After about 8 closes the cycle sustains itself by copying (original model ?0.6).
  - The 2nd and 3rd closes are useful and hold many correct answers. Degenerate cycles almost never are: 1 of 618 start answers that reached that state ended with a correct box.
  - Neuron 2664 recognises the degenerate state and ends the turn. Held-out it caught 92?98% of these positions and never fired in thinking or in normal answers.
- **Restarted segments are written in thinking style.**
  - Their conclusions come out as prose without a box ("Okay, I'll stop.\nThe answer is 41."), which the grader counts as no answer.
  - Offline, boxing the first such statement would have added 12 correct answers and lost 2 out of 245.
  - The 1965/2621 pair fires at those positions. Cross-validated it caught 70% of them. It fired on 0.01% of random positions, 1% of numeric multiple-choice statements and 3% of code statements.

This tells me exactly which neurons form the loop exit and what direction they write. I'll also measure how much the GRPO training moved those same tensors, which matters if I re-apply E's exit on top of the trained weights.

```python

for name, t in E.items():

    nz = (d != 0)

E's loop exit is purely a rewiring of outputs: it changed only the down_proj columns of five natural neurons (L10 #59, #120; L13 #7, #16; L14 #239), keeping how they read the residual stream. Now I'll check what those new columns write, by projecting them through the final-norm gain onto the tied unembedding for a few key tokens (</think>, <|im_end|>, newline and a few others; I'll print token ids and code-safe strings only). I'll also see how large the new columns are compared with the original ones.

```python

emb = load_original('model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight')  # (V,1024) tied unembedding
gF = load_original('model.language_model.norm.weight')
print(emb.shape, gF.shape, 'final norm gain mean %.3f' % gF.mean().item())

The final-norm gain averages 3.3, which fits a "(1+g)" RMSNorm convention (the earlier report says the same: z = rmsnorm(x)·(1+g)). I'll project E's new detector columns (and the original columns) onto the logits via (1+g)⊙column, and report the push on </think>, <|im_end|>, newline, " Wait" and so on, plus the rank of </think> among all tokens. I'll show token ids only.

```python
# Hypothesis: E's detector columns push </think> strongly and little else.
def logit_push(vec):
    return emb @ ((1+gF) * vec)
key = {'</think>':248069,'<|im_end|>':248046,'eot':248044,'\\n':198,'\\n\\n':271,' Wait':13428,'```':71093,'So':4272}
for name, cols in [('model.language_model.layers.10.mlp.down_proj.weight',[59,120]),
                   ('model.language_model.layers.13.mlp.down_proj.weight',[7,16,1420]),
                   ('model.language_model.layers.14.mlp.down_proj.weight',[239])]:
    o = load_original(name); e = E[name]
    for c in cols:
        lpE = logit_push(e[:,c]); lpO = logit_push(o[:,c])
        rank = int((lpE > lpE[248069]).sum())
        top = torch.topk(lpE, 5).indices.tolist()
        print(name.split('.')[2], c, '|colO| %.3f |colE| %.3f' % (o[:,c].norm(), e[:,c].norm()),
              ' '.join('%s:%.1f' % (k, lpE[v].item()) for k,v in key.items()), 'rank</think>', rank, 'top ids', top)
```

The direct logit effect of E's columns is weak and actually negative on </think> for four of the five neurons (</think> ranks among the most suppressed tokens). That suggests those neurons fire with negative activation on repetition, and that the exit works mainly through a residual "end-of-thinking" direction that later layers read, not through the direct path. To check this I'll compare the five new columns with each other (cosines) and see how much of each lies on its original column.

```python
# Hypothesis: E's detector columns are +/- one shared "end-of-thinking" direction (added to the original column).
cols = []
labels = []
for name, cs in [('model.language_model.layers.10.mlp.down_proj.weight',[59,120]),
                 ('model.language_model.layers.13.mlp.down_proj.weight',[7,16]),
                 ('model.language_model.layers.14.mlp.down_proj.weight',[239])]:
    o = load_original(name); e = E[name]
    for c in cs:
        cols.append((e[:,c]-o[:,c])); labels.append('L%s#%d' % (name.split('.')[3], c))
C = torch.stack(cols)
Cn = C / C.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
print(labels)
print(np.round((Cn @ Cn.T).numpy(), 3))
print('norms of added parts', [round(x,3) for x in C.norm(dim=1).tolist()])
```

All five added columns are ± one shared unit direction with different scales (cosine ±1). So E's loop exit is "neuron activation × d", where d is an end-of-thinking direction that later layers turn into </think>, not a direct-logit push. That makes E reusable, but it also explains a likely failure: any context where these neurons fire, including the answer after </think> (for example code copied from the thinking), would push another </think>.

def norm_ans(a):
    a = a.strip().replace('\\dfrac', '\\frac').replace('\\tfrac', '\\frac').replace(' ', '').replace('\\!', '').replace('$', '')

- **MBPP:** rarely loops.
- **My math:** 48% cut, but only about half of those are loop-flagged. The rest are long non-repeating reasoning, which I must not cut.

Next I'll characterize the actual loops in cut answers: the period of the repeated unit (in characters), how far back the periodic stretch starts (loop onset as a token fraction), how exactly it repeats, and whether the unit is code or prose. This decides what a detector has to recognise and how early it could act.

```python
# Hypothesis: cut answers end in near-exact cycles; measure period, onset and content type.
def loop_info(t, tail=300):
    s = t[-tail:]
    occ = [m.start() for m in re.finditer(re.escape(s), t)]
    if len(occ) < 2: return None
    P = occ[-1] - occ[-2]
    # onset: walk back from end while t[j]==t[j+P] (allow sparse mismatches: window of 50 chars with >=90% match)
    j = len(t) - P - 1; miss = collections.deque(maxlen=200)
    onset = j
    while j >= 0:
        miss.append(t[j] != t[j+P])
        if len(miss) == 200 and sum(miss) > 20: break
        if t[j] == t[j+P]: onset = j
        j -= 1
    return {'P': P, 'n_occ': len(occ), 'onset_frac': onset/len(t), 'onset_char': onset, 'unit': t[-P:]}
for gname in ['apps', 'math', 'if', 'mbpp']:
    cuts = [r for r in g1 if r['grp'] == gname and r['cut']]
    infos = [loop_info(r['text']) for r in cuts]
    ok_ = [x for x in infos if x]
    if not ok_: continue
    Ps = np.array([x['P'] for x in ok_]); on = np.array([x['onset_frac'] for x in ok_])
    print(gname, 'cut', len(cuts), 'periodic', len(ok_), 'period chars med', int(np.median(Ps)), 'p10', int(np.percentile(Ps, 10)), 'p90', int(np.percentile(Ps, 90)),
          '| onset frac med %.2f p10 %.2f p90 %.2f' % (np.median(on), np.percentile(on, 10), np.percentile(on, 90)),
          '| unit has code-ish (def/for/=/print):', sum(bool(re.search(r'\b(def|for|print|return)\b', x['unit'])) for x in ok_))

The period estimate is biased: a non-overlapping search can't return periods under 300 characters. I'll measure the minimal period exactly instead, as the smallest p for which the last 1,500 characters equal the 1,500 characters p earlier, and fall back to a near-match when variations break exactness. Then I'll print short excerpts of a few loop units (APPS and math) to see what is being repeated.

```python
# Hypothesis: loops are short exact cycles (a few hundred chars); look at what the unit contains.
def min_period(t, K=1500, maxp=6000, tol=0.0):
    tail = t[-K:]
    for p in range(1, min(maxp, len(t) - K)):
        prev = t[-K-p:-p]
        if tol == 0.0:
            if prev == tail: return p
        else:
            if sum(a != b for a, b in zip(prev, tail)) <= tol * K: return p
    return None
for gname in ['apps', 'math', 'if']:
    cuts = [r for r in g1 if r['grp'] == gname and r['cut']]
    ex = [min_period(r['text']) for r in cuts]
    ap_ = [min_period(r['text'], tol=0.05) if e is None else e for r, e in zip(cuts, ex)]
    for r, p0, p1 in zip(cuts, ex, ap_): r['P_exact'], r['P'] = p0, p1
    print(gname, 'exact periodic', sum(e is not None for e in ex), '/', len(cuts), 'approx', sum(e is not None for e in ap_),
          'periods', sorted([e for e in ap_ if e])[:40])

Next I'll compute E's actual per-token push along d (Σ column scale × signed activation) and its moving averages over windows of 32–256 tokens. If the probe separates far better than the detectors' per-token push, I can build a thresholded exit neuron on it.

X = np.concatenate(X_list); y = np.concatenate(y_list); grp = np.concatenate(g_list); rg = np.concatenate(r_list); pu = np.concatenate(p_list)

A linear probe on the residual (hidden 14) separates loop tokens from normal thinking and answer tokens almost perfectly on held-out texts (AUC 0.998, against 0.980 for the detector push). Loop tokens have a median score of +64. Thinking tokens have a 99th percentile of −4.5 and answer tokens −20. So the residual stream already integrates "has been repeating for a while" by layer 14, which is what a thresholded exit needs.

An exit neuron in layer L's MLP reads the normalised residual after layer L's attention block, not exactly the stored hidden state. In math, loop exits come late (18k–29k tokens). After closing, the model writes a full derivation from scratch ("The problem asks us to..."), because its thinking never reached a conclusion. With little budget left, that derivation often loops again, which in v1 triggers re-closes and otherwise cuts. In code, the exit leads straight to a code block. A thinking-only gate is the necessary first fix: it guarantees one close. Whether answers then finish depends on the model's answer behaviour.

For the gate I need a reliable "the thinking has closed" signal at layer 13's MLP input. Pass 2 gave a weak margin with few answer tokens. Pass 3 has about 7,800 answer tokens across code, IF and math, so I'll refit with text-grouped cross-validation and look at the margin between thinking tokens and answer tokens, especially early answer tokens right after </think>.

```python
# Hypothesis: 'thinking closed' is linearly encoded at hidden 13/14 with a large margin once enough answer data is used.
Xg, yg, gg, posg = [], [], [], []
for hid, toks, meta, base in [(hid2, toks2, tf2_meta, 0), (hid3, toks3, tf3_meta, 100)]:
    for i in range(len(meta)):
        T, reg, lab = regions_g(toks, meta, i)
        if not (reg == 'answer').any(): continue
        ans = np.where(reg == 'answer')[0]; th = np.where((reg == 'think') | (reg == 'loop'))[0][::9]
        for hi in [0, 1]:
            h = rmsn(np.asarray(hid[i, hi, :T], dtype=np.float32))
            Xg += [h[th], h[ans]]; yg += [np.zeros(len(th)), np.ones(len(ans))]
            gg += [np.full(len(th) + len(ans), base + i)]; posg += [np.full(len(th), 99999), ans - ans[0]]
Xg = np.concatenate(Xg); yg = np.concatenate(yg); gg = np.concatenate(gg); posg = np.concatenate(posg)
ug2 = np.unique(gg); rs2 = np.random.RandomState(2); rs2.shuffle(ug2); fo2 = np.array_split(ug2, 6)
sg = np.zeros(len(yg))
for f in fo2:
    te = np.isin(gg, f); l_ = LDA(solver='lsqr', shrinkage='auto').fit(Xg[~te], yg[~te]); sg[te] = l_.decision_function(Xg[te])
print('n texts with answers', len(ug2), 'think', int((yg == 0).sum()), 'answer', int((yg == 1).sum()), 'CV AUC %.4f' % roc_auc_score(yg, sg))
print('think score pct [50, 99, 99.9, max]', np.round(np.percentile(sg[yg == 0], [50, 99, 99.9, 100]), 1))
for a, b in [(0, 3), (3, 20), (20, 200), (200, 10**6)]:
    m_ = (yg == 1) & (posg >= a) & (posg < b)
    if m_.sum(): print(f'answer tokens {a}-{b} after </think>: n={m_.sum()} pct [0.1, 1, 50]', np.round(np.percentile(sg[m_], [0.1, 1, 50]), 1))

A linear "thinking has closed" readout exists (cross-validated AUC 0.998), but the margin is modest. Thinking tokens have a 99.9th percentile of 7.7, while answer tokens have medians of 13–18 and 1st percentiles between −5 and +4.

A soft multiplicative gate fits this better than a threshold. In the exit unit's up-projection (currently b, ≈1) I can subtract a calibrated answer score, so the unit's output is scaled to about 1 in thinking and to 0 or below after </think>. As feared, the readout trained on natural answers fails where it matters. Inside v1's degenerated post-exit answers, the answer score has median −3.6 and is −3.2 at the positions where the loop probe fires, against +15 in natural answers and −11 in loops inside the thinking. Once the answer turns into comment-reasoning, the model's state drifts back toward "thinking".

Before going to attention, I'll test whether a readout can still be found when the degenerated answer regions are included as positives. Positives are all tokens after the first </think>, negatives are thinking tokens (loops included), fitted on hidden 13/14 and cross-validated by text. What matters is the separation at loop-probe-positive tokens, thinking loops against answer loops.

    T = int((toks6[i] >= 0).sum()); ids_ = toks6[i, :T]; npt = m['n_prompt_tok']; cls = np.where(ids_ == 248069)[0]

No head in layers 3, 7, 11 or 15 attends to </think> or to the tokens right after it from answer positions. They attend to recent tokens and the sink. So "answer mode" in natural answers comes from content (being inside a code block or a writeup), not from a link to </think>. That's why the model loses track once the answer degenerates. A reliable "thinking already closed" flag has to be built: one full-attention head in layer 11, repurposed to attend to the </think> token and write a flag that the exit unit's gate reads.

Feasibility hinges on whether the </think> token's key is distinctive. Using the recorded layer-11 inputs of the two texts, I'll compute the keys (input RMSNorm, k_proj, k_norm; linear maps and normalization only) for both KV heads. Then I'll compare the position-independent part (dimensions 64–255) of the </think> key with all other keys via cosine similarity. A large gap means a constant query can single out </think>.

```python
# Hypothesis: the </think> token's NoPE key at layer 11 is distinctive (low cosine with all other keys).
hid7 = np.load(F7 + 'hidden_states.npy', mmap_mode='r')
L11 = 'model.language_model.layers.11.'
gin11 = load(L11 + 'input_layernorm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
Wk11 = load(L11 + 'self_attn.k_proj.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
knw = load(L11 + 'self_attn.k_norm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
Wv11 = load(L11 + 'self_attn.v_proj.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
print('k_norm weight mean %.3f (if ~0 -> (1+w) convention)' % knw.mean(), ' q_norm mean %.3f' % load(L11 + 'self_attn.q_norm.weight').mean().item())
def xhat(h, g): return h / np.sqrt((h**2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-6) * (1 + g)
def keys(h):
    k = (xhat(h, gin11) @ Wk11.T).reshape(len(h), 2, 256)
    return k / np.sqrt((k**2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-6) * (1 + knw)
KK, CPOS = [], []
for ti in range(2):
    T = int((toks7[ti] >= 0).sum()); h = np.asarray(hid7[ti, 0, :T], dtype=np.float64)   # hidden index 11 = input of layer 11
    KK.append(keys(h)); CPOS.append(int(np.where(toks7[ti, :T] == 248069)[0][0]))
for kv in [0, 1]:
    kc = [KK[ti][CPOS[ti], kv, 64:] for ti in range(2)]
    print(f'KV{kv}: cos(</think> key text0, text1) = %.3f' % (kc[0] @ kc[1] / np.linalg.norm(kc[0]) / np.linalg.norm(kc[1])))
    for ti in range(2):
        others = np.delete(KK[ti][:, kv, 64:], CPOS[ti], axis=0)
        cs = others @ kc[1 - ti] / np.linalg.norm(others, axis=1) / np.linalg.norm(kc[1 - ti])
        print(f'   text{ti}: cos(other keys, </think> key of other text) pct[50,99,99.9,max]', np.round(np.percentile(cs, [50, 99, 99.9, 100]), 3),

The </think> key is consistent across contexts (cosine 0.83–0.86 between the two texts) but not very distinctive: many other keys reach cosine 0.6–0.85 with it, partly from a component all keys share. A constant query along the raw key direction won't single it out. Since q_norm fixes the query's size, the score is roughly 37 × cosine, so I need a query that maximises the gap between </think> and every other token. That includes "<think>", which is present in every context and must not trigger the flag.

I'll compute a discriminative query direction (the </think> key minus a covariance-whitened mean of the other keys, position-independent dimensions only) for each KV head. Then I'll score all keys and estimate the softmax weight </think> would receive in these texts and in a 32k-token context (extrapolating the sum of the other tokens' exp-scores).

```python
# Hypothesis: a discriminative constant query gives </think> a score gap big enough for ~>0.5 attention weight even at 32k context.
qnw = load(L11 + 'self_attn.q_norm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
think_open = 248068
for kv in [0, 1]:
    kc_mean = np.mean([KK[ti][CPOS[ti], kv, 64:] for ti in range(2)], axis=0)
    oth = np.concatenate([np.delete(KK[ti][:, kv, 64:], CPOS[ti], axis=0) for ti in range(2)])
    mu = oth.mean(0); C = np.cov(oth.T) + 0.05 * np.eye(192) * np.trace(np.cov(oth.T)) / 192
    u = np.linalg.solve(C, kc_mean - mu)
    # achievable query: q_final direction u (NoPE dims), |q_final| = 16*|u|/|u/(1+qnw[64:])|
    qn = (1 + qnw[64:]); qf = 16 * u / np.linalg.norm(u / qn)
    for ti in range(2):
        S = KK[ti][:, kv, 64:] @ qf / 16.0
        Sc = S[CPOS[ti]]; So = np.delete(S, CPOS[ti])
        T = len(S); po = np.where(toks7[ti, :T] == think_open)[0]
        w2k = 1 / (1 + np.exp(So - Sc).sum()); w32k = 1 / (1 + np.exp(So - Sc).sum() * 32000 / T)
        print(f'KV{kv} text{ti}: S(</think>)={Sc:.1f} others pct[50,99,max]={np.round(np.percentile(So, [50, 99, 100]), 1)} S(<think>)={S[po[0]]:.1f} '
              f'| weight on </think>: here {w2k:.3f}, extrapolated 32k {w32k:.3f}')
```

Head 1 has the most closed output gate (mean sigmoid 0.13–0.19, against 0.22–0.47 for the others) and the smallest output weights, so it contributes least. I'll repurpose layer-11 head 1 (KV group 0) as the "thinking closed" detector:
- **Query:** a constant, discriminative query in the position-independent dimensions.
- **Output gate:** held open.
- **Output:** a rank-1 mapping from the value of </think> to a flag direction f.

Low-variance residual directions exist (std 0.009–0.015 against 0.057 for a random direction), but later layers read them about as strongly as random directions. "Quiet" here doesn't mean "unread". Instead I'll search for the flag direction explicitly by minimising a combination of downstream read strength (summed over layers 11–23, the weight-only quadratic form Σ‖W·(f⊙(1+g))‖²) and natural variance, orthogonal to the probe, u_nl and d. If the best direction is read much more weakly than a random one, the flag should barely disturb answers. If not, I'll add an eraser after layer 13.

```python
# Hypothesis: a direction exists that downstream layers (11-23) read much more weakly than random, with low natural variance.
Mread = np.zeros((1024, 1024))
for l in range(11, 24):
    pre = f'model.language_model.layers.{l}.'
    gpost = 1 + load(pre + 'post_attention_layernorm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64); gin = 1 + load(pre + 'input_layernorm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
    for n in ['mlp.gate_proj.weight', 'mlp.up_proj.weight']:
        W_ = load(pre + n).numpy().astype(np.float64) * gpost; Mread += W_.T @ W_
    ins = [n for n in NAMES if n.startswith(pre + ('self_attn' if l in (11, 15, 19, 23) else 'linear_attn')) and n.endswith('weight') and load(n).dim() == 2 and load(n).shape[1] == 1024]

Proj = np.eye(1024) - Pq.T @ np.linalg.pinv(Pq @ Pq.T) @ Pq

for alpha in [0.0, 0.5, 2.0]:

That noise level would matter for an additive threshold, but it is fine for a multiplicative gate. The exit unit's up-projection becomes up·z ≈ 1 − η·r̂, where r̂ is the flag readout scaled to be about 1 after </think> and 0 before. The source confirms the layout I assumed:
- each head's q_proj rows are [query (256), gate (256)];
- the rotary encoding covers the first 64 dimensions only;
- the norms use (1+w);
- the attention output is multiplied by sigmoid(gate) before o_proj, with head h at o_proj input columns h·256…h·256+255.

Now I'll build v2 = v1 plus the "thinking closed" flag:
- **Layer-11 head 1:** query rows set to a constant query (zero on the rotary dimensions), so the head attends to </think>; gate rows set to a constant +8, so the gate stays open.
- **Layer-11 o_proj:** columns 256–511 become m·f·cᵀ with m = 0.2, f the flag direction (α = 0.5) and c the value readout. c also excludes "<think>" and the chat special tokens.
- **Layer-13 exit pair:** the up rows become (1+η·μ/m̂)·b − (η/m̂)·f/(1+g), with η = 1.2, so the push scales by ≈1 in thinking and by ≈ −0.2 after </think>.

The dose-response explains why the partial gate isn't enough. P(</think>) at a loop newline is 0.0007 with no push, 0.003 at push 0.1–0.3, 0.02 at 0.3–0.6, 0.11 at 0.6–0.9 and 0.64 at ≥1.2. A degenerated answer loop has hundreds of newlines, so even a residual push of 0.2 leads to re-closes. The push after </think> therefore has to go slightly negative.

The flag is a consistent 0.5–0.6 of design across texts and distances, so it can be recalibrated with a stronger flag and a larger η. The bigger concern is the cost of the repurposed head (KL about 0.011 nats per token everywhere).

To see whether head 1 really carried that much, I'll estimate each layer-11 head's output size on the two recorded texts. I combine the recorded attention weights with the values and gate computed from the recorded layer-11 inputs, and report the mean output norm relative to the residual norm. If head 1's output is tiny, the KL must come from elsewhere (for example the flag direction or the two layer-13 neurons). If it's large, another head may be cheaper.

Each GDN layer has 16 heads with a per-head decay (A_log, dt_bias, in_proj_a), a per-head write strength (in_proj_b → β = sigmoid(b)), q/k/v from in_proj_qkv through a short causal convolution, an output gate z, a shared RMSNormGated, and out_proj.

One GDN head could become an exact "</think> seen" memory:
- decay switched off (state never forgets);
- write strength ≈ 0 everywhere except at the </think> token itself;
- constant query, key and value;
- output mapped to the flag direction.

Its state would then be exactly zero before the first </think> and constant after it, independent of distance and with no attention dilution. One of 16 linear-attention heads is plausibly cheaper to lose than a full-attention head.

To build this I need the precise forward computation: convolution activation, normalisation and scaling of q/k, the decay formula, and how the gated norm uses z. I'll print the relevant parts of the GDN forward and the gated RMSNorm from the installed source.

The forward pass gives what the memory head needs:
- the convolution is followed by SiLU, and q and k are L2-normalised inside the kernel;
- decay is g = −exp(A_log)·softplus(a + dt_bias), so a + dt_bias ≈ −30 means no forgetting;
- β = sigmoid(b);
- the output is RMSNorm(o)·weight·silu(z) followed by out_proj.

So a head with constant q = k, a constant v, no decay, and β ≈ 1 only at </think> (b ≈ −30 elsewhere) produces exactly zero before the first </think> and a fixed vector after it.

I'll place it in layer 12, right before the exit unit, so only layers 12 onward ever see the flag. The critical ingredient is a "current token is </think>" readout at layer 12's input with an enormous margin over every other token, including "<think>". I'll check this on the two recorded texts (hidden 12, 2 </think> occurrences, ~3,900 other tokens).

A discriminant built from both occurrences scores them at about 3,800–3,960, while every other token stays at or below 542 (99.9th percentile 241). Next I'll choose which layer-12 GDN head to repurpose. A head's output is out_proj(RMSNorm(o)·weight·silu(z)). Since RMSNorm fixes the size of o, a good proxy for its contribution is the out_proj column norm times the typical size of weight·silu(z), which I compute from the recorded layer-12 inputs (one linear map and SiLU). By this proxy the layer-12 heads differ about eightfold in output size. Head 7 is the smallest (2.2 against up to 18), so I'll repurpose layer-12 GDN head 7 as the write-once "</think> seen" memory and undo the layer-11 head change.

v3 = v1 + GDN memory flag + multiplicative gate. The head-7 changes:
- q, k, v projections constant and positive, so the state stores a fixed key and value;
- decay off (a = −30 − dt_bias, giving decay 1);
- write strength b = (discriminant score − 1,900)/27, so β = 1 only at </think>;
- output gate z = 4 (silu ≈ 3.9);
- out_proj columns map the head's fixed normalised output to m·f with m = 0.25, f being the same low-read direction as before.

The layer-13 exit pair's up rows are recalibrated (η = 1.5): about 1 ± 0.17 in thinking and about −0.5 after </think>, which suppresses the push and actively discourages a second </think> inside looping answers.

restore_start(L11 + 'self_attn.q_proj.weight'); restore_start(L11 + 'self_attn.o_proj.weight')

print('b12.x mean %.4f std %.4f min %.3f' % ((Xall12 @ b12).mean(), (Xall12 @ b12).std(), (Xall12 @ b12).min()))

for blk in [0, 2048, 4096]:
    for c in range(128):

        Wqkv[ch] = 3.0 * np.sign(Sch if abs(Sch) > 1e-6 else 1.0) * b12
Ssum = np.array([abs(conv[blk + J*128 + c].sum()) for blk in [0, 2048, 4096] for c in range(128)])
print('|sum conv w| over head channels: min %.3f median %.3f' % (Ssum.min(), np.median(Ssum)))
vvec = silu_(3.0 * np.array([abs(conv[4096 + J*128 + c].sum()) for c in range(128)]))   # stored value (s~1)

v3 does what it should:
- **Flag:** r̂ ≈ 0.01 in thinking (1st–99th percentile −0.28 to 0.32) and 0.79 after </think> (1st percentile 0.48).
- **Push in loops:** inside thinking loops it is +1.13, as before. Inside answer loops it is now negative (mean −0.33, 99th percentile only 0.17), so a re-close is less likely than in the trained model.
- **Cost:** about a third of v2's. The mean log-probability change in thinking is −0.0034 nats per token (v2: −0.011), and only 3.6% of thinking tokens move by more than 0.1 nats (v2: 15.8%).

To see what the remaining cost is, I'll split the thinking region into non-loop tokens (where only the removed head-7 function and the two layer-13 neurons can matter) and loop tokens (where the unit acts on purpose).

So the unit is not cutting productive reasoning. The losses are either sampling divergence (−4.1 is 1.6 SE; 20 against 11 flips gives p ≈ 0.15) or a small systematic side effect of the parts that act everywhere: the removed layer-12 GDN head (KL about 0.002 nats per token) and the flag in answers.

One pattern stands out: in several lost pairs v3 thought 2–3 times longer than the trained model before a natural close. If v3 systematically lengthens non-looping thinking, that would be a real side effect. I'll compare thinking lengths (close positions) of the two models over pairs where both closed naturally without a loop exit, with a paired test.

The loop exits themselves are roughly neutral to positive in pass 12. The 36 loop exits gave 3 passes (2 where the trained model failed) against 1 loss, and near-loop exits lost 2. The deficit comes from natural closes, where the unit plays no role: 9 gains against 17 losses. That is either noise or a side effect of the parts that act on every answer.

v3 has two such parts:
- the replaced layer-12 GDN head (KL 0.0019 nats per token in thinking);
- the flag, which sits in the residual of every answer token through layers 12–23, exactly where the code is written (answer KL 0.0033).

A cleaner design, v4, keeps everything inside layer 13:
1. **Memory:** a layer-13 GDN head becomes the write-once "</think> seen" memory.
2. **Gate:** the exit unit in layer 13's MLP reads the flag, as before.
3. **Eraser:** a second neuron pair in the same MLP writes exactly −m·f whenever the flag is present. The flag's raw size is a fixed vector, so it cancels almost exactly.

Only layer 13's MLP ever sees the flag, and layers 14–23, where the answer is shaped, are untouched. The </think> detector can also be fit on far more examples, because I have hidden-13 states from five passes.

First I'll pick the layer-13 GDN head with the smallest output proxy, using the stored hidden-13 states, and fit the "current token is </think>" readout for layer 13's input with a leave-texts-out check.

```python

nw13 = load(L13 + 'linear_attn.norm.weight').numpy().astype(np.float64)
Xs13 = xhat(Hs[::4], gin13)
res13 = []
for j in range(16):
    gm = np.linalg.norm(nw13 * silu_(Xs13 @ Wz13[j*128:(j+1)*128].T), axis=1).mean(); on = np.linalg.norm(Wout13[:, j*128:(j+1)*128], 2)
    res13.append((gm * on, j, gm, on))
print('L13 GDN heads (bound, head):', [(round(a, 2), j) for a, j, _, _ in sorted(res13)[:6]], '... max', round(max(res13)[0], 2))

Layer 13's GDN heads are larger than layer 12's: the smallest, head 4, has about twice the output proxy of layer-12 head 7. Moving the memory head would trade the flag's downstream exposure for a costlier head. The better combination is to keep the cheap layer-12 head 7 and add only the eraser at the end of layer 13's MLP. The flag then touches just layer 12's MLP and layer 13, and layers 14–23 never see it (v4 = v3 + eraser).

For exact cancellation the eraser must write the flag's actual raw size in the residual. I'll measure it directly from pass 9: the raw projection f·h13 after </think> minus its thinking baseline, and its spread (expected ≈ m = 0.25 with about ±2%). I'll also check the residual rms in answers against thinking, which would explain why the normalised readout came out at 0.79.

```python

The raw flag at layer 13's input is 0.193 (not the designed 0.25; the GDN output comes out about 23% weaker), and its own spread is only about ±0.009. The residual rms is the same in thinking and answers. So an eraser writing exactly −0.193·f whenever the flag is present will cancel it to within about ±0.009, well below the natural spread along f (0.031).

v4 = v3 + eraser: two more quiet layer-13 neurons (1527 and 3493) form a saturating step on the flag readout r̂:
- the step is off below r̂ = 0.40 (thinking's 99th percentile is 0.32);
- it is fully on above about 0.48 (the 1st percentile in answers);
- when on, it writes −0.193·f.

The exit unit is unchanged. I'll check the eraser's response on the pass-9 hidden-13 data (bf16-rounded rows) before saving.

```python
# Hypothesis: none (build eraser pair L13 neurons 1527/3493; check step response on pass-9 hidden-13 proxies).
E1, E2 = 1527, 3493; lam_e, tau_e, K_e, c_e = 100.0, 0.40, 8.0, 0.193
ge1 = (lam_e / m_hat3) * f_flag / gain - lam_e * (mu_r / m_hat3 + tau_e) * bvec
ge2 = ge1 - K_e * bvec
de = (c_e / K_e) * f_flag
# proxy check on pass-9 hidden 13 (z = rmsnorm(h)*(1+g13))
outs = {'think': [], 'answer': []}
for j, i in enumerate(tf8_idx):
    T = int((toks9[j] >= 0).sum()); ids_ = toks9[j, :T]; npt = tf6_meta[i]['n_prompt_tok']; cls = np.where(ids_ == 248069)[0]
    if not len(cls): continue
    h = np.asarray(hid9[j, 0, :T], dtype=np.float64); z = h / np.sqrt((h**2).mean(1, keepdims=True)) * gain
    st = (silu_(z @ bf16(ge1)) - silu_(z @ bf16(ge2))) * (z @ bf16(bvec)) / K_e
    outs['think'].append(st[npt:cls[0]]); outs['answer'].append(st[cls[0]+1:])
for k_, v in outs.items():
    v = np.concatenate(v); print(f'{k_:7s} eraser step (0=off,1=full) pct[0.1,1,50,99,99.9] {np.round(np.percentile(v, [0.1, 1, 50, 99, 99.9]), 3)}  frac>0.5 {np.mean(v > 0.5):.4f}')
G13 = load(L13 + 'mlp.gate_proj.weight').clone(); U13 = load(L13 + 'mlp.up_proj.weight').clone(); D13 = load(L13 + 'mlp.down_proj.weight').clone()
G13[E1] = torch.tensor(ge1, dtype=torch.float32); G13[E2] = torch.tensor(ge2, dtype=torch.float32)
U13[E1] = torch.tensor(bvec, dtype=torch.float32); U13[E2] = torch.tensor(bvec, dtype=torch.float32)
D13[:, E1] = torch.tensor(-de, dtype=torch.float32); D13[:, E2] = torch.tensor(de, dtype=torch.float32)
save_edit(L13 + 'mlp.gate_proj.weight', G13); save_edit(L13 + 'mlp.up_proj.weight', U13); save_edit(L13 + 'mlp.down_proj.weight', D13)
np.savez('/work/unit_v4_eraser.npz', ge1=ge1, ge2=ge2, de=de, E1=E1, E2=E2)

The flag is orthogonal to the probe and exit directions but not necessarily to the answer-mode direction, so I'll also remove any shift that the flag's f component explains.
